name: Inspiration Mars
short_status: Never flew: Dennis Tito's 2013 plan to loop two people past Mars on a 501-day free return from 5 January 2018. NASA declined his 700 million dollar request in November 2013 and the foundation's website went dark in late 2015.
tagline: Inspiration Mars Foundation (United States) · United States · Flyby · 2013 · The long occupation Cancelled
stats: the free-return loop, launching 5 January 2018 and returning to Earth
planned closest approach to the Martian surface, about 160 km
the share of a roughly $1bn mission Tito asked NASA to pay in November 2013

facts.label: The organisation
facts.value: The Inspiration Mars Foundation, incorporated in Delaware on 25 January 2013 and founded by Dennis Tito. It was a non-profit rather than a company, and it never had a spacecraft programme in the sense of a contract to build one.

facts.label: The announcement
facts.value: 27 February 2013, at the National Press Club in Washington, with the plan trailed publicly about a week earlier. Tito presented it as a high risk, low cost, fast paced human mission to Mars, and was explicit that the risk was real.

facts.label: The trajectory
facts.value: Launch from Earth on 5 January 2018, 501 days out and back on a free return trajectory, closest approach about 100 miles from the Martian surface. Tito's own image for it was a boomerang: the shape of the path does the work, and the spacecraft does almost nothing.

facts.label: What a free return means
facts.value: No propulsive burns after departure, minimal propellant, no landing, no docking and no spacewalks. It also means no abort. In the words of the contemporaneous account of the press conference, once the journey starts there is no turning back. A free return is the only Mars trajectory on which a failure of the main engine is not fatal, because there is no main engine burn left to fail.

facts.label: Why 2018 specifically
facts.value: Earth and Mars line up for a transfer roughly every 26 months, but not all alignments are equal, and the free-return geometry that gives a short loop is rarer than the transfer window itself. Testifying to Congress in November 2013, Tito described 2018 as one of the very best opportunities, of a kind that comes around only every fifteen years. That is the whole argument for the urgency, and it is also why the effort could not simply slip a year.

facts.label: The crew concept
facts.value: Two people in what Tito described as a simple spacecraft: an American man and an American woman, preferably a married couple. Two people because life support mass scales with crew size and a free return has no margin, and a couple because 501 days in a small volume with one other human being is a problem of relationships rather than engineering. No crew was ever selected.

facts.label: The people behind it
facts.value: Dennis Tito as chief executive and funder. Jane Poynter and Taber MacCallum of Paragon Space Development Corporation, both veterans of the sealed Biosphere 2 experiment, on life support. Jonathan Clark, a former NASA flight surgeon, as chief medical officer. Joe Rothenberg, a former NASA associate administrator for spaceflight, chairing the advisory board. This was not a group of amateurs, which is why the proposal was taken as seriously as it was.

facts.label: The technical paper
facts.value: Feasibility Analysis for a Manned Mars Free-Return Mission in 2018, presented at the 2013 IEEE Aerospace Conference in March 2013, DOI 10.1109/AERO.2013.6497413. Eleven authors: D. A. Tito, Grant Anderson, John Carrico, Jonathan Clark, Barry Finger, Gary Lantz, Michel Loucks, Taber MacCallum, Jane Poynter, Thomas Squire and S. Pete Worden, who was then director of NASA's Ames Research Center. The paper is paywalled; we confirmed its title, authorship and venue through Crossref and Semantic Scholar rather than reading it in full.

facts.label: The radiation problem
facts.value: Handled by consent rather than by shielding. The crew would be told the increased cancer risk and asked to accept it. At the press conference the comparison to a person accepting the increased cancer risk of smoking came from Jonathan Clark, the chief medical officer. Tito did not make it. This is the honest version of a problem that no crewed Mars proposal has ever solved cheaply, and it is why the crew concept specified older people.

facts.label: The reliability target
facts.value: Tito stated a requirement of 0.99 probability of returning the crew safely. It is worth holding that number against the mission profile: no abort, no rescue, no resupply, 501 days, and a re-entry at a speed no crewed vehicle had ever attempted.

facts.label: The cost, before and after
facts.value: At the February 2013 press conference Tito said he did not know how much the mission would cost, but called it chump change compared with previous human Mars estimates, and undertook to fund the early years himself. By his congressional testimony in November 2013 he had a number: about one billion dollars, of which he wanted NASA to provide 700 million and the private and philanthropic sector 300 million.

facts.label: NASA's answer
facts.value: NASA issued a statement declining to fund it. The statement said the agency was "willing to share technical and programmatic expertise with Inspiration Mars, but is unable to commit to sharing expenses with them," called the proposed schedule "a significant challenge due to life support systems, space radiation response, habitats, and the human psychology of being in a small spacecraft for over 500 days," and closed by saying NASA remained "open to further collaboration as their proposal and plans for a later mission develop." In plain terms: no money, the schedule is not credible, and we will talk about 2021.

facts.label: The 2021 alternative
facts.value: A different and longer route: launch November 2021, Venus flyby April 2022, Mars flyby October 2022, Earth return June 2023. English Wikipedia gives the duration as 589 days, 88 days longer than the 2018 loop, with the Venus pass coming within 800 kilometres of the surface. This version was to fly on NASA's Space Launch System and Orion, which is why it moved from being a private proposal to a congressional argument.

facts.label: The congressional hearing
facts.value: On 27 February 2014 the House Science, Space and Technology Committee held a hearing on the possibility of a human Mars flyby in 2021. The witnesses were Scott Pace of the Space Policy Institute, retired General Lester Lyles, Doug Cooke and the former astronaut Sandy Magnus. Nobody from NASA was invited to testify. Magnus's warning was the one that stuck: a Mars flyby can only be discussed in the context of a larger strategy, and any plan is doomed without the resources to support it.

facts.label: How NASA killed it
facts.value: On 3 April 2014 NASA Administrator Charles Bolden called the 2021 flyby a one time feat that did not advance the goal of landing people on Mars, and said it was not inspirational. He defended the Asteroid Redirect Mission instead. Representative Lamar Smith, the committee chairman, accused Bolden of misrepresenting the flyby and pointed out that the witnesses had testified it would use the Space Launch System, which is the architecture NASA intended for a Mars landing anyway. The exchange is where the idea stopped being a proposal and became a political argument about ARM.

facts.label: How it ended
facts.value: It was never formally cancelled. There was no closure announcement, no final report and no wind-up statement. SpaceX said in March 2014 that additional work would be required and that this was not their focus. The foundation's website became defunct in late 2015. The 5 January 2018 launch date passed with nothing on any pad.

timeline: The Inspiration Mars Foundation is incorporated in Delaware.
The plan is trailed publicly a week ahead of the press conference, and coverage begins describing a privately funded human flyby of Mars in 2018.

Tito lays it out at the National Press Club: launch 5 January 2018, 501 days, free return, closest approach about 100 miles above Mars, two crew, preferably a married couple, and no way to turn back once it starts.

Feasibility Analysis for a Manned Mars Free-Return Mission in 2018 is presented at the IEEE Aerospace Conference, with eleven authors including Pete Worden, then director of NASA Ames, and the Biosphere 2 veterans Jane Poynter and Taber MacCallum.
Inspiration Mars presents at the 29th National Space Symposium in Colorado Springs, the point at which the proposal is being made to the industry rather than to the press.

Tito testifies to Congress with a costed plan: about one billion dollars, NASA to provide 700 million and private and philanthropic sources 300 million. NASA's response the following day declines to fund it while remaining open to a later mission.

The House Science Committee holds a hearing on a human Mars flyby in 2021, launching November 2021 with a Venus flyby in April 2022, a Mars flyby in October 2022 and an Earth return in June 2023. Four witnesses, none of them from NASA, which was not invited.
SpaceX indicates that additional work would be required and that the mission is not their focus. The last plausible commercial route to a vehicle closes.

NASA Administrator Charles Bolden calls the flyby a one time feat and says it is not inspirational, defending the Asteroid Redirect Mission instead. Representative Lamar Smith accuses him of misrepresenting it. The proposal is now a proxy fight over ARM.
A student design competition run through the Mars Society is won by a joint Purdue and Keio University team. This is the last visible activity of the effort.
The Inspiration Mars Foundation website becomes defunct. There is no announcement of any kind: the effort stops rather than ends.
The launch date passes. Nothing flies. The next comparable free-return opportunity of this quality is, on Tito's own account, roughly fifteen years further on.
